n(Zn) = 6.5/65.4 = 0.0994 mol; 1:1 ratio; m = 0.0994 x 63.5 = 6.3 g, which the working rounds to 6.4 g with 63.55.

options.explanation: Side reactions divert reactant.

questions.stem: A crystallisation experiment reports a 104% yield. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The reaction exceeded its theoretical limit

options.text: The Mr used was too large

questions.stem: State the percentage yield equation and the source of each input.
questions.modelAnswer: Percentage yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100; the actual yield is measured experimentally and the theoretical yield comes from a reacting-mass calculation.

questions.stem: State the theoretical copper yield from 6.5 g of zinc in the displacement example.
questions.modelAnswer: 0.0994 mol of zinc maps 1:1 to 0.0994 mol of copper, about 6.4 g at 63.55 g mol^-1.

questions.stem: Explain why percentage yield can exceed 100% even though atoms are conserved.
questions.modelAnswer: The percentage compares a MEASURED mass against a calculated ceiling, and the measured mass counts everything on the balance - solvent still trapped in damp crystals, impurities co-crystallised, or the filter paper weighed in error - so the number can pass 100 without any atom being created.

questions.stem: In the zinc and copper(II) sulfate displacement, 6.5 g of zinc yields 4.8 g of copper recovered. Calculate the percentage yield.
questions.modelAnswer: Theoretical copper = 0.0994 mol x 63.55 = 6.4 g (2 s.f.); percentage yield = 4.8 / 6.4 x 100 = 75%.

options.text: The sodium and bromine atoms exit as the by-product NaBr instead of entering the ethanol

questions.stem: Which statement about atom economy is correct?

options.text: Atom economy applies only to industrial reactions
options.explanation: It applies to any balanced equation.

options.text: A single-product reaction always runs at 100% atom economy
options.explanation: With no by-product, every reactant atom lands in the product.

options.explanation: The two metrics are independent.

questions.modelAnswer: Atom economy = (molecular mass of the desired product / sum of molecular masses of ALL reactants) x 100.

questions.stem: State the atom economy of any addition reaction and justify it in one sentence.
questions.modelAnswer: 100% - every atom of every reactant is incorporated into the single product, leaving no by-product.

questions.stem: Explain why atom economy can be calculated without any experiment.
questions.modelAnswer: The metric compares formula masses written into the balanced equation itself: the desired product's Mr over the reactants' combined Mr, both coefficients included; since the equation fixes where every atom can go, the efficiency of atom use is a bookkeeping property, not a measurement.
